r12-dc4-boundary.title: Draw the boundary: which divergence modes are/aren't caught
r12-dc4-boundary.imperative: State plainly which divergence modes this property catches and which it does not (truncation/re-wrapping/re-encoding/stripping on the MCP side; a divergence in only one arm's rendering path). BLOCK if the property is materially weaker than DC4 claims. Record pass/fail.
r12-dc4-boundary.finding: BOUNDARY, drawn from reading mcp_spine_server.py's real code plus my own mutation (r10): the MCP arm's pipeline after the shared engine call is run_engine() (capture stdout+stderr via redirect) -> as_result() (wrap into {content:[{text}], isError}) -> json.dumps over the JSON-RPC line -> ServerInstance.recv/status_text (json.loads, pull content[0].text). The CLI arm never touches any of that -- its stdout is read directly off its own subprocess. CATCHES (proven, not just argued): truncating (empirically proven -- my as_result() mutation cut 30 chars off the ACTIVE line's imperative and 4/5 tests went red on an AssertionError naming the exact byte mismatch); stripping (same mechanism -- any content removed from the ACTIVE line's imperative substring on the MCP side is caught, since the comparison is byte-exact against extract_imperative's captured group); re-wrapping (any prefix/suffix landing INSIDE the ACTIVE line -- not merely appended after it in trailing rail text, see below -- is caught the same way); re-encoding (any corruption introduced by run_engine's stdout+stderr concatenation, as_result's JSON wrapping, or ServerInstance's json.loads round-trip would show up as a byte difference in the same captured substring). A divergence in 'only one arm's rendering path' -- yes, caught, and in fact this IS what the property is actually testing: the MCP arm is the only one with a wrapping/transport layer at all (the CLI arm is a bare  call with no wrapper of its own), so 'one arm diverges' in practice always means the MCP side. DOES NOT CATCH: a bug inside the SHARED checklist_engine.main()/render_human() function itself, because both arms call that literal same Python function (CLI via its own subprocess's __main__, MCP via an in-process import-and-call) -- a corruption there renders identically wrong on both sides, so cli_imp==mcp_imp would still hold and this test would stay green. This is explicitly and correctly OUT of DC4's own stated scope ('the CLI projection and MCP tool result carry the SAME imperative text' -- same-but-wrong is not a DC4 violation by DC4's own wording; a shared-engine-correctness bug needs a different test, e.g. one that checks against the source template field). NON-BLOCKING OBSERVATION for triage: SingleGateWiringTests additionally asserts cli_imp/mcp_imp against gate.task['imperative'] (ground truth vs source) for its ONE canary gate (g1-implement) -- PopulationPropertyTests does NOT extend that ground-truth-vs-source check across the other 60 gates, only CLI-vs-MCP agreement. Not a DC4 gap (DC4 only requires CLI==MCP), but means a shared-render corruption affecting only some gates (not g1-implement) would slip past every check in this file. Verdict: the property is NOT weaker than DC4 claims -- it is exactly as strong as DC4's own wording requires, empirically proven sensitive to the real MCP-door-side divergence modes named in the handoff (truncate/re-wrap/re-encode/strip), and its one blind spot is a different, out-of-scope claim (shared-engine correctness) that DC4's own wording does not cover. PASS -- not a BLOCK.

PopulationPropertyTests (the 61-gate loop) only checks cli_imp==mcp_imp; it does not extend SingleGateWiringTests' ground-truth-vs-source-template check (cli_imp==gate.task['imperative'] and mcp_imp==gate.task['imperative']) across the population.
